system.description:
Maisons de Dwálin et de Thrár — Barbes-de-Feu et Torses-Larges

Les Maisons de Dwálin et de Thrár, connues respectivement comme celles des Barbes-de-Feu et des Torses-Larges, comptent parmi les plus anciennes lignées des Khazâd. Leurs Pères s’éveillèrent dans l’Ouest de la Terre du Milieu, au voisinage des Montagnes Bleues, et leurs descendants y fondèrent des royaumes souterrains bien avant l’établissement durable des grandes puissances humaines.

Les Barbes-de-Feu

Les Barbes-de-Feu tirent leur nom des teintes rousses, cuivrées ou rouge sombre fréquemment rencontrées dans leurs chevelures et leurs barbes. Ils sont associés aux grandes forges, au travail des métaux, aux armes richement décorées et à un tempérament plus vif que celui des autres Khazâd.

Ils excellent dans la forge, la fonte, la fabrication d’armes, les alliages, l’émaillage et les ornements métalliques.

Les Torses-Larges

Les Torses-Larges sont réputés pour leur carrure massive, leurs épaules puissantes et leur remarquable endurance. Ils sont particulièrement associés à la taille de pierre, aux grands ouvrages souterrains, aux fortifications, aux salles monumentales et aux travaux exigeant patience et force.

Ils excellent dans la maçonnerie, l’architecture, le creusement des salles, les fortifications, les ponts et les grands mécanismes.

Les royaumes des Montagnes Bleues

Les deux Maisons établirent leurs plus anciens royaumes dans les Montagnes Bleues. Leurs cités comprenaient salles royales, quartiers claniques, ateliers, forges, entrepôts, sanctuaires, tombeaux, ouvrages défensifs et routes creusées dans la montagne.

La proximité de leurs domaines favorisa les échanges de techniques, les mariages et la défense commune, mais provoqua aussi des querelles portant sur les filons, les droits de passage et la préséance des lignées.

Ruines, exils et continuité

Les guerres et bouleversements des Âges anciens détruisirent plusieurs de leurs grandes demeures. Les survivants se dispersèrent, fondèrent des colonies secondaires ou rejoignirent d’autres communautés khazâd. Les anciens sites ne furent pourtant jamais totalement abandonnés et devinrent des destinations de pèlerinage.

Le Nan-i-Naugrim

Le nom Nan-i-Naugrim, la « Vallée des Nains », fut appliqué à plusieurs régions successives liées aux établissements des deux Maisons. Pour les Khazâd, un nom peut désigner non seulement un lieu, mais aussi la continuité d’un peuple, d’un royaume ou d’une mémoire déplacée avec ses habitants.

Apparence et ornements

Les membres de ces Maisons sont courts, trapus et puissamment bâtis. Leur teint est généralement clair. Les cheveux et les barbes peuvent être noirs, brun sombre, roux ou rouge profond.

Les ornements de barbe indiquent la Maison, le clan, le métier, le rang, l’état matrimonial, un serment, une campagne militaire ou un deuil. Les Barbes-de-Feu apprécient le cuivre, l’or rouge et le bronze ; les Torses-Larges préfèrent souvent l’argent, le fer sombre et l’acier.

Vêtements et endurance

Leurs vêtements sont lourds, chauds et adaptés aux montagnes. Ils portent tuniques épaisses, braies solides, bottes renforcées, manteaux de laine, capes à capuchon vivement colorées, tabliers de cuir et ceintures chargées d’outils.

Leur endurance est considérable. Ils peuvent porter de lourdes charges, travailler durant de nombreuses heures et supporter des privations que peu d’autres peuples toléreraient.

Résistance au feu et au froid

Les deux Maisons possèdent une résistance remarquable aux températures extrêmes. Elles supportent mieux que la plupart des peuples la chaleur des forges, les vapeurs brûlantes des galeries et le froid des hauts cols.

Vision et maîtrise des cavernes

Comme les autres Khazâd, ils voient exceptionnellement bien dans l’obscurité. Ils savent évaluer la stabilité d’une voûte, la direction d’une galerie, la circulation de l’air, la proximité de l’eau, la qualité d’un filon et les risques d’éboulement.

Crainte de l’eau libre

Malgré leur endurance, ils craignent les grandes étendues d’eau et se montrent profondément mal à l’aise face à la mer, aux lacs profonds et aux rivières trop larges. La plupart ne savent pas nager et préfèrent ponts, tunnels et passages aménagés aux embarcations.

Société et lignées

La famille, le clan et la Maison définissent l’identité de chaque individu. Les rivalités internes suivent généralement des règles précises : arbitrage, duel rituel, compensation ou médiation des anciens plutôt qu’une guerre ouverte.

Le mariage est monogame, et la filiation suit traditionnellement la lignée masculine. Les femmes naines conservent néanmoins leur identité familiale et peuvent exercer une influence considérable.

Ancêtres et Mahal

Les deux Maisons croient que chaque lignée partage un esprit commun reliant tous ses membres. Les ancêtres sont révérés au-dessus de toute autre puissance, à l’exception de Mahal, leur créateur. La dévotion se manifeste par le travail bien accompli, la conservation des techniques, la solidité des ouvrages, la discipline, l’enseignement aux apprentis et la fidélité aux serments.

Tempérament, serments et offenses

Ils sont généralement sobres, silencieux, possessifs, soupçonneux, combatifs et introspectifs. Ils concluent les accords avec une extrême prudence et n’oublient ni une faveur ni une offense. Une dette peut être remboursée par les descendants longtemps après la mort des premiers protagonistes.

Commerce et guerre

Ils échangent armes, outils, armures, bijoux, pierre taillée et services d’ingénierie contre nourriture, bois, cuir, textiles et produits agricoles.

Au combat, ils sont tenaces et impitoyables. Les Barbes-de-Feu privilégient haches, marteaux et combats offensifs ; les Torses-Larges excellent dans les murs de boucliers, la défense des portes, les armures lourdes et les combats dans les tunnels.

Relations

Les Maisons de Dwálin et de Thrár entretiennent une proximité particulière, forgée par la géographie, les exils et les combats communs. Leurs relations avec la Maison de Durin sont respectueuses, mais non dépourvues de rivalité. Elles reconnaissent le prestige des Longues-Barbes sans toujours accepter leur prétention implicite à parler au nom de tous les Khazâd.

Formation culturelle

La Culture favorise particulièrement :

  • Minage
  • Spéléologie
  • Forge
  • Métallurgie
  • Maçonnerie
  • Architecture
  • Évaluation des minerais
  • Résistance
  • Développement corporel
  • Manœuvres en armure
  • Haches
  • Marteaux
  • Arbalètes
  • Connaissance souterraine
  • Histoire des clans
  • Généalogie
  • Commerce
  • Travail du cuir et de la pierre

Place dans la création de personnage

Cette Culture convient à un Khazâd issu des anciennes cités des Montagnes Bleues, du Nan-i-Naugrim, d’une colonie minière occidentale, d’un atelier de forgerons barbes-de-feu ou d’une lignée de bâtisseurs torses-larges.

Ensemble, les deux Maisons portent l’héritage occidental des Khazâd : celui de royaumes détruits mais jamais oubliés, de cités déplacées sans que leur mémoire disparaisse et de lignées convaincues qu’aucune ruine n’est réellement abandonnée tant qu’un seul Nain revient encore y prononcer le nom de ses ancêtres.

en.name: Khazâd (Houses of Dwálin and Thrár) — Firebeards and Broadbeams

system.description:
Khazâd (Houses of Dwálin and Thrár) — Firebeards and Broadbeams

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár, known respectively as the Firebeards and Broadbeams, are among the oldest lineages of the Khazâd. Their Fathers awoke in the West of Middle-earth near the Blue Mountains, and their descendants founded underground kingdoms there long before the great human powers established themselves permanently.

The Firebeards

The Firebeards take their name from the red, copper or dark-red colouring frequently found in their hair and beards. They are associated with great forges, metalworking, richly decorated weapons and a more fiery temperament than many other Khazâd.

They excel in smithing, smelting, weapon-making, alloys, enamelling and metal ornament.

The Broadbeams

The Broadbeams are renowned for their massive build, powerful shoulders and remarkable endurance. They are particularly associated with stonecutting, great underground works, fortifications, monumental halls and tasks requiring patience and strength.

They excel in masonry, architecture, excavating halls, fortification, bridges and large mechanisms.

The kingdoms of the Blue Mountains

The two Houses established their oldest kingdoms in the Blue Mountains. Their cities contained royal halls, clan quarters, workshops, forges, warehouses, sanctuaries, tombs, defensive works and roads cut through the mountain.

The proximity of their domains encouraged the exchange of techniques, intermarriage and mutual defence, but also caused disputes over mineral veins, rights of passage and precedence among lineages.

Ruins, exiles and continuity

The wars and upheavals of the Elder Days destroyed several of their great dwellings. Survivors scattered, founded secondary colonies or joined other Khazâd communities. Yet the old sites were never entirely abandoned and became destinations for pilgrimage.

The Nan-i-Naugrim

The name Nan-i-Naugrim, the “Vale of the Dwarves”, was applied to several successive regions connected with settlements of the two Houses. To the Khazâd, a name may designate not only a place, but the continuity of a people, a kingdom or a memory carried with its inhabitants when they move.

Appearance and ornament

Members of these Houses are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their complexion is generally fair. Hair and beards may be black, dark brown, red or deep red.

Beard ornaments indicate House, clan, craft, rank, marital status, an oath, a military campaign or mourning. Firebeards favour copper, red gold and bronze; Broadbeams often prefer silver, dark iron and steel.

Clothing and endurance

Their clothing is heavy, warm and suited to mountain life. They wear thick tunics, sturdy breeches, reinforced boots, woollen coats, brightly coloured hooded cloaks, leather aprons and belts laden with tools.

Their endurance is considerable. They can carry heavy loads, work for many hours and withstand deprivation that few other peoples could tolerate.

Resistance to fire and cold

Both Houses possess remarkable resistance to extreme temperatures. Better than most peoples, they endure the heat of forges, burning vapours in galleries and the cold of high mountain passes.

Vision and mastery of caverns

Like other Khazâd, they see exceptionally well in darkness. They know how to assess the stability of a vault, the direction of a passage, the flow of air, the proximity of water, the quality of a vein and the risk of collapse.

Fear of open water

Despite their endurance, they fear great expanses of water and feel deeply uncomfortable before the sea, deep lakes and very broad rivers. Most cannot swim and prefer bridges, tunnels and engineered crossings to boats.

Society and lineages

Family, clan and House define each individual's identity. Internal rivalries generally follow precise rules: arbitration, ritual duel, compensation or mediation by elders rather than open warfare.

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. Dwarven women nevertheless retain their family identity and may exercise considerable influence.

Ancestors and Mahal

Both Houses believe that each lineage shares a common spirit linking all its members. Ancestors are revered above every power except Mahal, their maker. Devotion is expressed through work well done, preservation of techniques, sound construction, discipline, teaching apprentices and faithfulness to oaths.

Temperament, oaths and offences

They are generally sober, quiet, possessive, suspicious, combative and introspective. They make agreements with extreme caution and forget neither a favour nor an offence. A debt may be repaid by descendants long after the original parties are dead.

Trade and war

They exchange weapons, tools, armour, jewellery, dressed stone and engineering services for food, timber, leather, textiles and agricultural produce.

In battle they are tenacious and merciless. Firebeards favour axes, hammers and offensive fighting; Broadbeams excel in shield walls, the defence of gates, heavy armour and tunnel warfare.

Relations

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár maintain a particular closeness forged by geography, exile and common wars. Their relations with the House of Durin are respectful but not without rivalry. They recognise the prestige of the Longbeards without always accepting their implicit claim to speak for all Khazâd.

Cultural training

The Culture particularly favours:

  • Mining
  • Caving
  • Smithing
  • Metallurgy
  • Masonry
  • Architecture
  • Ore Appraisal
  • Resistance
  • Body Development
  • Maneuvering in Armor
  • Axes
  • Hammers
  • Crossbows
  • Underground Lore
  • Clan History
  • Genealogy
  • Trading
  • Leatherwork and Stonecraft

Place in character creation

This Culture is appropriate for a Khazâd from the ancient cities of the Blue Mountains, the Nan-i-Naugrim, a western mining colony, a workshop of Firebeard smiths or a lineage of Broadbeam builders.

Together, the two Houses carry the western legacy of the Khazâd: kingdoms destroyed but never forgotten, cities moved without their memory disappearing, and lineages convinced that no ruin is truly abandoned while even one Dwarf still returns to speak the names of their ancestors there.

system.description:
Khazâd (Houses of Dwálin and Thrár) — Firebeards and Broadbeams

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár, known respectively as the Firebeards and Broadbeams, are among the oldest lineages of the Khazâd. Their Fathers awoke in the West of Middle-earth near the Blue Mountains, and their descendants founded underground kingdoms there long before the great human powers established themselves permanently.

The Firebeards

The Firebeards take their name from the red, copper or dark-red colouring frequently found in their hair and beards. They are associated with great forges, metalworking, richly decorated weapons and a more fiery temperament than many other Khazâd.

They excel in smithing, smelting, weapon-making, alloys, enamelling and metal ornament.

The Broadbeams

The Broadbeams are renowned for their massive build, powerful shoulders and remarkable endurance. They are particularly associated with stonecutting, great underground works, fortifications, monumental halls and tasks requiring patience and strength.

They excel in masonry, architecture, excavating halls, fortification, bridges and large mechanisms.

The kingdoms of the Blue Mountains

The two Houses established their oldest kingdoms in the Blue Mountains. Their cities contained royal halls, clan quarters, workshops, forges, warehouses, sanctuaries, tombs, defensive works and roads cut through the mountain.

The proximity of their domains encouraged the exchange of techniques, intermarriage and mutual defence, but also caused disputes over mineral veins, rights of passage and precedence among lineages.

Ruins, exiles and continuity

The wars and upheavals of the Elder Days destroyed several of their great dwellings. Survivors scattered, founded secondary colonies or joined other Khazâd communities. Yet the old sites were never entirely abandoned and became destinations for pilgrimage.

The Nan-i-Naugrim

The name Nan-i-Naugrim, the “Vale of the Dwarves”, was applied to several successive regions connected with settlements of the two Houses. To the Khazâd, a name may designate not only a place, but the continuity of a people, a kingdom or a memory carried with its inhabitants when they move.

Appearance and ornament

Members of these Houses are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their complexion is generally fair. Hair and beards may be black, dark brown, red or deep red.

Beard ornaments indicate House, clan, craft, rank, marital status, an oath, a military campaign or mourning. Firebeards favour copper, red gold and bronze; Broadbeams often prefer silver, dark iron and steel.

Clothing and endurance

Their clothing is heavy, warm and suited to mountain life. They wear thick tunics, sturdy breeches, reinforced boots, woollen coats, brightly coloured hooded cloaks, leather aprons and belts laden with tools.

Their endurance is considerable. They can carry heavy loads, work for many hours and withstand deprivation that few other peoples could tolerate.

Resistance to fire and cold

Both Houses possess remarkable resistance to extreme temperatures. Better than most peoples, they endure the heat of forges, burning vapours in galleries and the cold of high mountain passes.

Vision and mastery of caverns

Like other Khazâd, they see exceptionally well in darkness. They know how to assess the stability of a vault, the direction of a passage, the flow of air, the proximity of water, the quality of a vein and the risk of collapse.

Fear of open water

Despite their endurance, they fear great expanses of water and feel deeply uncomfortable before the sea, deep lakes and very broad rivers. Most cannot swim and prefer bridges, tunnels and engineered crossings to boats.

Society and lineages

Family, clan and House define each individual's identity. Internal rivalries generally follow precise rules: arbitration, ritual duel, compensation or mediation by elders rather than open warfare.

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. Dwarven women nevertheless retain their family identity and may exercise considerable influence.

Ancestors and Mahal

Both Houses believe that each lineage shares a common spirit linking all its members. Ancestors are revered above every power except Mahal, their maker. Devotion is expressed through work well done, preservation of techniques, sound construction, discipline, teaching apprentices and faithfulness to oaths.

Temperament, oaths and offences

They are generally sober, quiet, possessive, suspicious, combative and introspective. They make agreements with extreme caution and forget neither a favour nor an offence. A debt may be repaid by descendants long after the original parties are dead.

Trade and war

They exchange weapons, tools, armour, jewellery, dressed stone and engineering services for food, timber, leather, textiles and agricultural produce.

In battle they are tenacious and merciless. Firebeards favour axes, hammers and offensive fighting; Broadbeams excel in shield walls, the defence of gates, heavy armour and tunnel warfare.

Relations

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár maintain a particular closeness forged by geography, exile and common wars. Their relations with the House of Durin are respectful but not without rivalry. They recognise the prestige of the Longbeards without always accepting their implicit claim to speak for all Khazâd.

Cultural training

The Culture particularly favours:

  • Mining
  • Caving
  • Smithing
  • Metallurgy
  • Masonry
  • Architecture
  • Ore Appraisal
  • Resistance
  • Body Development
  • Maneuvering in Armor
  • Axes
  • Hammers
  • Crossbows
  • Underground Lore
  • Clan History
  • Genealogy
  • Trading
  • Leatherwork and Stonecraft

Place in character creation

This Culture is appropriate for a Khazâd from the ancient cities of the Blue Mountains, the Nan-i-Naugrim, a western mining colony, a workshop of Firebeard smiths or a lineage of Broadbeam builders.

Together, the two Houses carry the western legacy of the Khazâd: kingdoms destroyed but never forgotten, cities moved without their memory disappearing, and lineages convinced that no ruin is truly abandoned while even one Dwarf still returns to speak the names of their ancestors there.

system.description:
Khazâd (Houses of Dwálin and Thrár) — Firebeards and Broadbeams

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár, known respectively as the Firebeards and Broadbeams, are among the oldest lineages of the Khazâd. Their Fathers awoke in the West of Middle-earth near the Blue Mountains, and their descendants founded underground kingdoms there long before the great human powers established themselves permanently.

The Firebeards

The Firebeards take their name from the red, copper or dark-red colouring frequently found in their hair and beards. They are associated with great forges, metalworking, richly decorated weapons and a more fiery temperament than many other Khazâd.

They excel in smithing, smelting, weapon-making, alloys, enamelling and metal ornament.

The Broadbeams

The Broadbeams are renowned for their massive build, powerful shoulders and remarkable endurance. They are particularly associated with stonecutting, great underground works, fortifications, monumental halls and tasks requiring patience and strength.

They excel in masonry, architecture, excavating halls, fortification, bridges and large mechanisms.

The kingdoms of the Blue Mountains

The two Houses established their oldest kingdoms in the Blue Mountains. Their cities contained royal halls, clan quarters, workshops, forges, warehouses, sanctuaries, tombs, defensive works and roads cut through the mountain.

The proximity of their domains encouraged the exchange of techniques, intermarriage and mutual defence, but also caused disputes over mineral veins, rights of passage and precedence among lineages.

Ruins, exiles and continuity

The wars and upheavals of the Elder Days destroyed several of their great dwellings. Survivors scattered, founded secondary colonies or joined other Khazâd communities. Yet the old sites were never entirely abandoned and became destinations for pilgrimage.

The Nan-i-Naugrim

The name Nan-i-Naugrim, the “Vale of the Dwarves”, was applied to several successive regions connected with settlements of the two Houses. To the Khazâd, a name may designate not only a place, but the continuity of a people, a kingdom or a memory carried with its inhabitants when they move.

Appearance and ornament

Members of these Houses are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their complexion is generally fair. Hair and beards may be black, dark brown, red or deep red.

Beard ornaments indicate House, clan, craft, rank, marital status, an oath, a military campaign or mourning. Firebeards favour copper, red gold and bronze; Broadbeams often prefer silver, dark iron and steel.

Clothing and endurance

Their clothing is heavy, warm and suited to mountain life. They wear thick tunics, sturdy breeches, reinforced boots, woollen coats, brightly coloured hooded cloaks, leather aprons and belts laden with tools.

Their endurance is considerable. They can carry heavy loads, work for many hours and withstand deprivation that few other peoples could tolerate.

Resistance to fire and cold

Both Houses possess remarkable resistance to extreme temperatures. Better than most peoples, they endure the heat of forges, burning vapours in galleries and the cold of high mountain passes.

Vision and mastery of caverns

Like other Khazâd, they see exceptionally well in darkness. They know how to assess the stability of a vault, the direction of a passage, the flow of air, the proximity of water, the quality of a vein and the risk of collapse.

Fear of open water

Despite their endurance, they fear great expanses of water and feel deeply uncomfortable before the sea, deep lakes and very broad rivers. Most cannot swim and prefer bridges, tunnels and engineered crossings to boats.

Society and lineages

Family, clan and House define each individual's identity. Internal rivalries generally follow precise rules: arbitration, ritual duel, compensation or mediation by elders rather than open warfare.

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. Dwarven women nevertheless retain their family identity and may exercise considerable influence.

Ancestors and Mahal

Both Houses believe that each lineage shares a common spirit linking all its members. Ancestors are revered above every power except Mahal, their maker. Devotion is expressed through work well done, preservation of techniques, sound construction, discipline, teaching apprentices and faithfulness to oaths.

Temperament, oaths and offences

They are generally sober, quiet, possessive, suspicious, combative and introspective. They make agreements with extreme caution and forget neither a favour nor an offence. A debt may be repaid by descendants long after the original parties are dead.

Trade and war

They exchange weapons, tools, armour, jewellery, dressed stone and engineering services for food, timber, leather, textiles and agricultural produce.

In battle they are tenacious and merciless. Firebeards favour axes, hammers and offensive fighting; Broadbeams excel in shield walls, the defence of gates, heavy armour and tunnel warfare.

Relations

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár maintain a particular closeness forged by geography, exile and common wars. Their relations with the House of Durin are respectful but not without rivalry. They recognise the prestige of the Longbeards without always accepting their implicit claim to speak for all Khazâd.

Cultural training

The Culture particularly favours:

  • Mining
  • Caving
  • Smithing
  • Metallurgy
  • Masonry
  • Architecture
  • Ore Appraisal
  • Resistance
  • Body Development
  • Maneuvering in Armor
  • Axes
  • Hammers
  • Crossbows
  • Underground Lore
  • Clan History
  • Genealogy
  • Trading
  • Leatherwork and Stonecraft

Place in character creation

This Culture is appropriate for a Khazâd from the ancient cities of the Blue Mountains, the Nan-i-Naugrim, a western mining colony, a workshop of Firebeard smiths or a lineage of Broadbeam builders.

Together, the two Houses carry the western legacy of the Khazâd: kingdoms destroyed but never forgotten, cities moved without their memory disappearing, and lineages convinced that no ruin is truly abandoned while even one Dwarf still returns to speak the names of their ancestors there.

La proximité de leurs domaines favorisa les échanges de techniques, les mariages et la défense commune, mais provoqua aussi des querelles portant sur les filons, les droits de passage et la préséance des lignées.

Les guerres et bouleversements des Âges anciens détruisirent plusieurs de leurs grandes demeures. Les survivants se dispersèrent, fondèrent des colonies secondaires ou rejoignirent d’autres communautés khazâd. Les anciens sites ne furent pourtant jamais totalement abandonnés et devinrent des destinations de pèlerinage.

Le nom Nan-i-Naugrim, la « Vallée des Nains », fut appliqué à plusieurs régions successives liées aux établissements des deux Maisons. Pour les Khazâd, un nom peut désigner non seulement un lieu, mais aussi la continuité d’un peuple, d’un royaume ou d’une mémoire déplacée avec ses habitants.

Les membres de ces Maisons sont courts, trapus et puissamment bâtis. Leur teint est généralement clair. Les cheveux et les barbes peuvent être noirs, brun sombre, roux ou rouge profond.

Comme les autres Khazâd, ils voient exceptionnellement bien dans l’obscurité. Ils savent évaluer la stabilité d’une voûte, la direction d’une galerie, la circulation de l’air, la proximité de l’eau, la qualité d’un filon et les risques d’éboulement.

Crainte de l’eau libre

Malgré leur endurance, ils craignent les grandes étendues d’eau et se montrent profondément mal à l’aise face à la mer, aux lacs profonds et aux rivières trop larges. La plupart ne savent pas nager et préfèrent ponts, tunnels et passages aménagés aux embarcations.

La famille, le clan et la Maison définissent l’identité de chaque individu. Les rivalités internes suivent généralement des règles précises : arbitrage, duel rituel, compensation ou médiation des anciens plutôt qu’une guerre ouverte.

Le mariage est monogame, et la filiation suit traditionnellement la lignée masculine. Les femmes naines conservent néanmoins leur identité familiale et peuvent exercer une influence considérable.

Les deux Maisons croient que chaque lignée partage un esprit commun reliant tous ses membres. Les ancêtres sont révérés au-dessus de toute autre puissance, à l’exception de Mahal, leur créateur. La dévotion se manifeste par le travail bien accompli, la conservation des techniques, la solidité des ouvrages, la discipline, l’enseignement aux apprentis et la fidélité aux serments.

Ils sont généralement sobres, silencieux, possessifs, soupçonneux, combatifs et introspectifs. Ils concluent les accords avec une extrême prudence et n’oublient ni une faveur ni une offense. Une dette peut être remboursée par les descendants longtemps après la mort des premiers protagonistes.

Ils échangent armes, outils, armures, bijoux, pierre taillée et services d’ingénierie contre nourriture, bois, cuir, textiles et produits agricoles.

  • Maçonnerie

  • Manœuvres en armure

system.description:
Khazâd (Houses of Dwálin and Thrár) — Firebeards and Broadbeams

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár, known respectively as the Firebeards and Broadbeams, are among the oldest lineages of the Khazâd. Their Fathers awoke in the West of Middle-earth near the Blue Mountains, and their descendants founded underground kingdoms there long before the great human powers established themselves permanently.

The Firebeards

The Firebeards take their name from the red, copper or dark-red colouring frequently found in their hair and beards. They are associated with great forges, metalworking, richly decorated weapons and a more fiery temperament than many other Khazâd.

They excel in smithing, smelting, weapon-making, alloys, enamelling and metal ornament.

The Broadbeams

The Broadbeams are renowned for their massive build, powerful shoulders and remarkable endurance. They are particularly associated with stonecutting, great underground works, fortifications, monumental halls and tasks requiring patience and strength.

They excel in masonry, architecture, excavating halls, fortification, bridges and large mechanisms.

The kingdoms of the Blue Mountains

The two Houses established their oldest kingdoms in the Blue Mountains. Their cities contained royal halls, clan quarters, workshops, forges, warehouses, sanctuaries, tombs, defensive works and roads cut through the mountain.

The proximity of their domains encouraged the exchange of techniques, intermarriage and mutual defence, but also caused disputes over mineral veins, rights of passage and precedence among lineages.

Ruins, exiles and continuity

The wars and upheavals of the Elder Days destroyed several of their great dwellings. Survivors scattered, founded secondary colonies or joined other Khazâd communities. Yet the old sites were never entirely abandoned and became destinations for pilgrimage.

The Nan-i-Naugrim

The name Nan-i-Naugrim, the “Vale of the Dwarves”, was applied to several successive regions connected with settlements of the two Houses. To the Khazâd, a name may designate not only a place, but the continuity of a people, a kingdom or a memory carried with its inhabitants when they move.

Appearance and ornament

Members of these Houses are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their complexion is generally fair. Hair and beards may be black, dark brown, red or deep red.

Beard ornaments indicate House, clan, craft, rank, marital status, an oath, a military campaign or mourning. Firebeards favour copper, red gold and bronze; Broadbeams often prefer silver, dark iron and steel.

Clothing and endurance

Their clothing is heavy, warm and suited to mountain life. They wear thick tunics, sturdy breeches, reinforced boots, woollen coats, brightly coloured hooded cloaks, leather aprons and belts laden with tools.

Their endurance is considerable. They can carry heavy loads, work for many hours and withstand deprivation that few other peoples could tolerate.

Resistance to fire and cold

Both Houses possess remarkable resistance to extreme temperatures. Better than most peoples, they endure the heat of forges, burning vapours in galleries and the cold of high mountain passes.

Vision and mastery of caverns

Like other Khazâd, they see exceptionally well in darkness. They know how to assess the stability of a vault, the direction of a passage, the flow of air, the proximity of water, the quality of a vein and the risk of collapse.

Fear of open water

Despite their endurance, they fear great expanses of water and feel deeply uncomfortable before the sea, deep lakes and very broad rivers. Most cannot swim and prefer bridges, tunnels and engineered crossings to boats.

Society and lineages

Family, clan and House define each individual's identity. Internal rivalries generally follow precise rules: arbitration, ritual duel, compensation or mediation by elders rather than open warfare.

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. Dwarven women nevertheless retain their family identity and may exercise considerable influence.

Ancestors and Mahal

Both Houses believe that each lineage shares a common spirit linking all its members. Ancestors are revered above every power except Mahal, their maker. Devotion is expressed through work well done, preservation of techniques, sound construction, discipline, teaching apprentices and faithfulness to oaths.

Temperament, oaths and offences

They are generally sober, quiet, possessive, suspicious, combative and introspective. They make agreements with extreme caution and forget neither a favour nor an offence. A debt may be repaid by descendants long after the original parties are dead.

Trade and war

They exchange weapons, tools, armour, jewellery, dressed stone and engineering services for food, timber, leather, textiles and agricultural produce.

In battle they are tenacious and merciless. Firebeards favour axes, hammers and offensive fighting; Broadbeams excel in shield walls, the defence of gates, heavy armour and tunnel warfare.

Relations

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár maintain a particular closeness forged by geography, exile and common wars. Their relations with the House of Durin are respectful but not without rivalry. They recognise the prestige of the Longbeards without always accepting their implicit claim to speak for all Khazâd.

Cultural training

The Culture particularly favours:

  • Mining
  • Caving
  • Smithing
  • Metallurgy
  • Masonry
  • Architecture
  • Ore Appraisal
  • Resistance
  • Body Development
  • Maneuvering in Armor
  • Axes
  • Hammers
  • Crossbows
  • Underground Lore
  • Clan History
  • Genealogy
  • Trading
  • Leatherwork and Stonecraft

Place in character creation

This Culture is appropriate for a Khazâd from the ancient cities of the Blue Mountains, the Nan-i-Naugrim, a western mining colony, a workshop of Firebeard smiths or a lineage of Broadbeam builders.

Together, the two Houses carry the western legacy of the Khazâd: kingdoms destroyed but never forgotten, cities moved without their memory disappearing, and lineages convinced that no ruin is truly abandoned while even one Dwarf still returns to speak the names of their ancestors there.

Maisons de Dwálin et de Thrár — Barbes-de-Feu et Torses-Larges

Les Maisons de Dwálin et de Thrár, connues respectivement comme celles des Barbes-de-Feu et des Torses-Larges, comptent parmi les plus anciennes lignées des Khazâd. Leurs Pères s’éveillèrent dans l’Ouest de la Terre du Milieu, au voisinage des Montagnes Bleues, et leurs descendants y fondèrent des royaumes souterrains bien avant l’établissement durable des grandes puissances humaines.

Les Barbes-de-Feu

Les Barbes-de-Feu tirent leur nom des teintes rousses, cuivrées ou rouge sombre fréquemment rencontrées dans leurs chevelures et leurs barbes. Ils sont associés aux grandes forges, au travail des métaux, aux armes richement décorées et à un tempérament plus vif que celui des autres Khazâd.

Ils excellent dans la forge, la fonte, la fabrication d’armes, les alliages, l’émaillage et les ornements métalliques.

Les Torses-Larges

Les Torses-Larges sont réputés pour leur carrure massive, leurs épaules puissantes et leur remarquable endurance. Ils sont particulièrement associés à la taille de pierre, aux grands ouvrages souterrains, aux fortifications, aux salles monumentales et aux travaux exigeant patience et force.

Ils excellent dans la maçonnerie, l’architecture, le creusement des salles, les fortifications, les ponts et les grands mécanismes.

Les royaumes des Montagnes Bleues

Les deux Maisons établirent leurs plus anciens royaumes dans les Montagnes Bleues. Leurs cités comprenaient salles royales, quartiers claniques, ateliers, forges, entrepôts, sanctuaires, tombeaux, ouvrages défensifs et routes creusées dans la montagne.

La proximité de leurs domaines favorisa les échanges de techniques, les mariages et la défense commune, mais provoqua aussi des querelles portant sur les filons, les droits de passage et la préséance des lignées.

Ruines, exils et continuité

Les guerres et bouleversements des Âges anciens détruisirent plusieurs de leurs grandes demeures. Les survivants se dispersèrent, fondèrent des colonies secondaires ou rejoignirent d’autres communautés khazâd. Les anciens sites ne furent pourtant jamais totalement abandonnés et devinrent des destinations de pèlerinage.

Le Nan-i-Naugrim

Le nom Nan-i-Naugrim, la « Vallée des Nains », fut appliqué à plusieurs régions successives liées aux établissements des deux Maisons. Pour les Khazâd, un nom peut désigner non seulement un lieu, mais aussi la continuité d’un peuple, d’un royaume ou d’une mémoire déplacée avec ses habitants.

Apparence et ornements

Les membres de ces Maisons sont courts, trapus et puissamment bâtis. Leur teint est généralement clair. Les cheveux et les barbes peuvent être noirs, brun sombre, roux ou rouge profond.

Les ornements de barbe indiquent la Maison, le clan, le métier, le rang, l’état matrimonial, un serment, une campagne militaire ou un deuil. Les Barbes-de-Feu apprécient le cuivre, l’or rouge et le bronze ; les Torses-Larges préfèrent souvent l’argent, le fer sombre et l’acier.

Vêtements et endurance

Leurs vêtements sont lourds, chauds et adaptés aux montagnes. Ils portent tuniques épaisses, braies solides, bottes renforcées, manteaux de laine, capes à capuchon vivement colorées, tabliers de cuir et ceintures chargées d’outils.

Leur endurance est considérable. Ils peuvent porter de lourdes charges, travailler durant de nombreuses heures et supporter des privations que peu d’autres peuples toléreraient.

Résistance au feu et au froid

Les deux Maisons possèdent une résistance remarquable aux températures extrêmes. Elles supportent mieux que la plupart des peuples la chaleur des forges, les vapeurs brûlantes des galeries et le froid des hauts cols.

Vision et maîtrise des cavernes

Comme les autres Khazâd, ils voient exceptionnellement bien dans l’obscurité. Ils savent évaluer la stabilité d’une voûte, la direction d’une galerie, la circulation de l’air, la proximité de l’eau, la qualité d’un filon et les risques d’éboulement.

Crainte de l’eau libre

Malgré leur endurance, ils craignent les grandes étendues d’eau et se montrent profondément mal à l’aise face à la mer, aux lacs profonds et aux rivières trop larges. La plupart ne savent pas nager et préfèrent ponts, tunnels et passages aménagés aux embarcations.

Société et lignées

La famille, le clan et la Maison définissent l’identité de chaque individu. Les rivalités internes suivent généralement des règles précises : arbitrage, duel rituel, compensation ou médiation des anciens plutôt qu’une guerre ouverte.

Le mariage est monogame, et la filiation suit traditionnellement la lignée masculine. Les femmes naines conservent néanmoins leur identité familiale et peuvent exercer une influence considérable.

Ancêtres et Mahal

Les deux Maisons croient que chaque lignée partage un esprit commun reliant tous ses membres. Les ancêtres sont révérés au-dessus de toute autre puissance, à l’exception de Mahal, leur créateur. La dévotion se manifeste par le travail bien accompli, la conservation des techniques, la solidité des ouvrages, la discipline, l’enseignement aux apprentis et la fidélité aux serments.

Tempérament, serments et offenses

Ils sont généralement sobres, silencieux, possessifs, soupçonneux, combatifs et introspectifs. Ils concluent les accords avec une extrême prudence et n’oublient ni une faveur ni une offense. Une dette peut être remboursée par les descendants longtemps après la mort des premiers protagonistes.

Ils échangent armes, outils, armures, bijoux, pierre taillée et services d’ingénierie contre nourriture, bois, cuir, textiles et produits agricoles.

system.description:
Khazâd (Houses of Dwálin and Thrár) — Firebeards and Broadbeams

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár, known respectively as the Firebeards and Broadbeams, are among the oldest lineages of the Khazâd. Their Fathers awoke in the West of Middle-earth near the Blue Mountains, and their descendants founded underground kingdoms there long before the great human powers established themselves permanently.

The Firebeards

The Firebeards take their name from the red, copper or dark-red colouring frequently found in their hair and beards. They are associated with great forges, metalworking, richly decorated weapons and a more fiery temperament than many other Khazâd.

They excel in smithing, smelting, weapon-making, alloys, enamelling and metal ornament.

The Broadbeams

The Broadbeams are renowned for their massive build, powerful shoulders and remarkable endurance. They are particularly associated with stonecutting, great underground works, fortifications, monumental halls and tasks requiring patience and strength.

They excel in masonry, architecture, excavating halls, fortification, bridges and large mechanisms.

The kingdoms of the Blue Mountains

The two Houses established their oldest kingdoms in the Blue Mountains. Their cities contained royal halls, clan quarters, workshops, forges, warehouses, sanctuaries, tombs, defensive works and roads cut through the mountain.

The proximity of their domains encouraged the exchange of techniques, intermarriage and mutual defence, but also caused disputes over mineral veins, rights of passage and precedence among lineages.

Ruins, exiles and continuity

The wars and upheavals of the Elder Days destroyed several of their great dwellings. Survivors scattered, founded secondary colonies or joined other Khazâd communities. Yet the old sites were never entirely abandoned and became destinations for pilgrimage.

The Nan-i-Naugrim

The name Nan-i-Naugrim, the “Vale of the Dwarves”, was applied to several successive regions connected with settlements of the two Houses. To the Khazâd, a name may designate not only a place, but the continuity of a people, a kingdom or a memory carried with its inhabitants when they move.

Appearance and ornament

Members of these Houses are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their complexion is generally fair. Hair and beards may be black, dark brown, red or deep red.

Beard ornaments indicate House, clan, craft, rank, marital status, an oath, a military campaign or mourning. Firebeards favour copper, red gold and bronze; Broadbeams often prefer silver, dark iron and steel.

Clothing and endurance

Their clothing is heavy, warm and suited to mountain life. They wear thick tunics, sturdy breeches, reinforced boots, woollen coats, brightly coloured hooded cloaks, leather aprons and belts laden with tools.

Their endurance is considerable. They can carry heavy loads, work for many hours and withstand deprivation that few other peoples could tolerate.

Resistance to fire and cold

Both Houses possess remarkable resistance to extreme temperatures. Better than most peoples, they endure the heat of forges, burning vapours in galleries and the cold of high mountain passes.

Vision and mastery of caverns

Like other Khazâd, they see exceptionally well in darkness. They know how to assess the stability of a vault, the direction of a passage, the flow of air, the proximity of water, the quality of a vein and the risk of collapse.

Fear of open water

Despite their endurance, they fear great expanses of water and feel deeply uncomfortable before the sea, deep lakes and very broad rivers. Most cannot swim and prefer bridges, tunnels and engineered crossings to boats.

Society and lineages

Family, clan and House define each individual's identity. Internal rivalries generally follow precise rules: arbitration, ritual duel, compensation or mediation by elders rather than open warfare.

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. Dwarven women nevertheless retain their family identity and may exercise considerable influence.

Ancestors and Mahal

Both Houses believe that each lineage shares a common spirit linking all its members. Ancestors are revered above every power except Mahal, their maker. Devotion is expressed through work well done, preservation of techniques, sound construction, discipline, teaching apprentices and faithfulness to oaths.

Temperament, oaths and offences

They are generally sober, quiet, possessive, suspicious, combative and introspective. They make agreements with extreme caution and forget neither a favour nor an offence. A debt may be repaid by descendants long after the original parties are dead.

Trade and war

They exchange weapons, tools, armour, jewellery, dressed stone and engineering services for food, timber, leather, textiles and agricultural produce.

In battle they are tenacious and merciless. Firebeards favour axes, hammers and offensive fighting; Broadbeams excel in shield walls, the defence of gates, heavy armour and tunnel warfare.

Relations

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár maintain a particular closeness forged by geography, exile and common wars. Their relations with the House of Durin are respectful but not without rivalry. They recognise the prestige of the Longbeards without always accepting their implicit claim to speak for all Khazâd.

Cultural training

The Culture particularly favours:

  • Mining
  • Caving
  • Smithing
  • Metallurgy
  • Masonry
  • Architecture
  • Ore Appraisal
  • Resistance
  • Body Development
  • Maneuvering in Armor
  • Axes
  • Hammers
  • Crossbows
  • Underground Lore
  • Clan History
  • Genealogy
  • Trading
  • Leatherwork and Stonecraft

Place in character creation

This Culture is appropriate for a Khazâd from the ancient cities of the Blue Mountains, the Nan-i-Naugrim, a western mining colony, a workshop of Firebeard smiths or a lineage of Broadbeam builders.

Together, the two Houses carry the western legacy of the Khazâd: kingdoms destroyed but never forgotten, cities moved without their memory disappearing, and lineages convinced that no ruin is truly abandoned while even one Dwarf still returns to speak the names of their ancestors there.

Khazâd (Houses of Dwálin and Thrár) — Firebeards and Broadbeams

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár, known respectively as the Firebeards and Broadbeams, are among the oldest lineages of the Khazâd. Their Fathers awoke in the West of Middle-earth near the Blue Mountains, and their descendants founded underground kingdoms there long before the great human powers established themselves permanently.

The Firebeards

The Firebeards take their name from the red, copper or dark-red colouring frequently found in their hair and beards. They are associated with great forges, metalworking, richly decorated weapons and a more fiery temperament than many other Khazâd.

They excel in smithing, smelting, weapon-making, alloys, enamelling and metal ornament.

The Broadbeams

The Broadbeams are renowned for their massive build, powerful shoulders and remarkable endurance. They are particularly associated with stonecutting, great underground works, fortifications, monumental halls and tasks requiring patience and strength.

They excel in masonry, architecture, excavating halls, fortification, bridges and large mechanisms.

The kingdoms of the Blue Mountains

The two Houses established their oldest kingdoms in the Blue Mountains. Their cities contained royal halls, clan quarters, workshops, forges, warehouses, sanctuaries, tombs, defensive works and roads cut through the mountain.

The proximity of their domains encouraged the exchange of techniques, intermarriage and mutual defence, but also caused disputes over mineral veins, rights of passage and precedence among lineages.

Ruins, exiles and continuity

The wars and upheavals of the Elder Days destroyed several of their great dwellings. Survivors scattered, founded secondary colonies or joined other Khazâd communities. Yet the old sites were never entirely abandoned and became destinations for pilgrimage.

The Nan-i-Naugrim

The name Nan-i-Naugrim, the “Vale of the Dwarves”, was applied to several successive regions connected with settlements of the two Houses. To the Khazâd, a name may designate not only a place, but the continuity of a people, a kingdom or a memory carried with its inhabitants when they move.

Appearance and ornament

Members of these Houses are short, stocky and powerfully built. Their complexion is generally fair. Hair and beards may be black, dark brown, red or deep red.

Beard ornaments indicate House, clan, craft, rank, marital status, an oath, a military campaign or mourning. Firebeards favour copper, red gold and bronze; Broadbeams often prefer silver, dark iron and steel.

Clothing and endurance

Their clothing is heavy, warm and suited to mountain life. They wear thick tunics, sturdy breeches, reinforced boots, woollen coats, brightly coloured hooded cloaks, leather aprons and belts laden with tools.

Their endurance is considerable. They can carry heavy loads, work for many hours and withstand deprivation that few other peoples could tolerate.

Resistance to fire and cold

Both Houses possess remarkable resistance to extreme temperatures. Better than most peoples, they endure the heat of forges, burning vapours in galleries and the cold of high mountain passes.

Vision and mastery of caverns

Like other Khazâd, they see exceptionally well in darkness. They know how to assess the stability of a vault, the direction of a passage, the flow of air, the proximity of water, the quality of a vein and the risk of collapse.

Fear of open water

Despite their endurance, they fear great expanses of water and feel deeply uncomfortable before the sea, deep lakes and very broad rivers. Most cannot swim and prefer bridges, tunnels and engineered crossings to boats.

Society and lineages

Family, clan and House define each individual's identity. Internal rivalries generally follow precise rules: arbitration, ritual duel, compensation or mediation by elders rather than open warfare.

Marriage is monogamous, and descent traditionally follows the male line. Dwarven women nevertheless retain their family identity and may exercise considerable influence.

Ancestors and Mahal

Both Houses believe that each lineage shares a common spirit linking all its members. Ancestors are revered above every power except Mahal, their maker. Devotion is expressed through work well done, preservation of techniques, sound construction, discipline, teaching apprentices and faithfulness to oaths.

Temperament, oaths and offences

They are generally sober, quiet, possessive, suspicious, combative and introspective. They make agreements with extreme caution and forget neither a favour nor an offence. A debt may be repaid by descendants long after the original parties are dead.

Trade and war

They exchange weapons, tools, armour, jewellery, dressed stone and engineering services for food, timber, leather, textiles and agricultural produce.

In battle they are tenacious and merciless. Firebeards favour axes, hammers and offensive fighting; Broadbeams excel in shield walls, the defence of gates, heavy armour and tunnel warfare.

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár maintain a particular closeness forged by geography, exile and common wars. Their relations with the House of Durin are respectful but not without rivalry. They recognise the prestige of the Longbeards without always accepting their implicit claim to speak for all Khazâd.

  • Mining
  • Caving
  • Smithing
  • Metallurgy
  • Masonry
  • Architecture
  • Ore Appraisal
  • Resistance
  • Body Development
  • Maneuvering in Armor
  • Axes
  • Hammers
  • Crossbows
  • Underground Lore
  • Clan History
  • Genealogy
  • Trading
  • Leatherwork and Stonecraft

This Culture is appropriate for a Khazâd from the ancient cities of the Blue Mountains, the Nan-i-Naugrim, a western mining colony, a workshop of Firebeard smiths or a lineage of Broadbeam builders.

Both Houses believe that each lineage shares a common spirit linking all its members. Ancestors are revered above every power except Mahal, their maker. Devotion is expressed through work well done, preservation of techniques, sound construction, discipline, teaching apprentices and faithfulness to oaths.

Temperament, oaths and offences

They are generally sober, quiet, possessive, suspicious, combative and introspective. They make agreements with extreme caution and forget neither a favour nor an offence. A debt may be repaid by descendants long after the original parties are dead.

Trade and war

They exchange weapons, tools, armour, jewellery, dressed stone and engineering services for food, timber, leather, textiles and agricultural produce.

In battle they are tenacious and merciless. Firebeards favour axes, hammers and offensive fighting; Broadbeams excel in shield walls, the defence of gates, heavy armour and tunnel warfare.

Relations

The Houses of Dwálin and Thrár maintain a particular closeness forged by geography, exile and common wars. Their relations with the House of Durin are respectful but not without rivalry. They recognise the prestige of the Longbeards without always accepting their implicit claim to speak for all Khazâd.

Cultural training

The Culture particularly favours:

  • Mining
  • Caving
  • Smithing
  • Metallurgy
  • Masonry
  • Architecture
  • Ore Appraisal
  • Resistance
  • Body Development
  • Maneuvering in Armor
  • Axes
  • Hammers
  • Crossbows
  • Underground Lore
  • Clan History
  • Genealogy
  • Trading
  • Leatherwork and Stonecraft

Place in character creation

This Culture is appropriate for a Khazâd from the ancient cities of the Blue Mountains, the Nan-i-Naugrim, a western mining colony, a workshop of Firebeard smiths or a lineage of Broadbeam builders.

Together, the two Houses carry the western legacy of the Khazâd: kingdoms destroyed but never forgotten, cities moved without their memory disappearing, and lineages convinced that no ruin is truly abandoned while even one Dwarf still returns to speak the names of their ancestors there.
